reconcile.connective: Defenders deny the buried premise: Genesis 11:26 lists Abram first for dignity, so Terah was 130 (not 70) when Abram was born, leaving him 75 at Haran.

discrepancy.connective: The objection was pressed early by the Karaite polemicist Isaac of Troki, who held that Stephen erred in Acts 7:4 — that on the plain reading of Genesis 11:26 Abram left Haran while Terah was still alive, not after his death.

skeptic.name: Isaac ben Abraham of Troki
skeptic.attribution: Isaac ben Abraham of Troki (d. 1594), Chizzuk Emunah (Faith Strengthened), part 2, ch. 61 (1593)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Many have been greatly puzzled with the account here, supposing because Abram is mentioned first, that therefore he was the eldest son of Terah: but he is only put first by way of dignity. … Terah died two hundred and five years old, Gen 11:32; then Abram departed from Haran when seventy-five years old, Gen 12:4; therefore Abram was born, not when his father Terah was seventy, but when he was one hundred and thirty.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly dissolves the chronological chain the contradiction is built on: it denies that Gen 11:26 means Terah was 70 at Abram's birth (the false premise SAB itself identifies), placing Abram's birth at Terah 130 so that 75 at Haran + Terah's death at 205 are mutually consistent. Two non-adjacent verbatim sentences joined sense-preservingly; ends on a real source period.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Genesis 11:26
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this exact chronology directly, arguing Abram is named first only 'by way of dignity' and was born when Terah was 130, not 70, so 75 at Haran reconciles with Terah's death at 205 (Acts 7:4). Used as the row's harmonizing anchor since Haley's specific-passage coverage could not be confirmed by search.
